Iteration
When we want to reuse code, we can use:

functions to save the steps of the task
iteration to apply that function to new inputs

Let’s talk about iteration in R.

Iterating using a for loop & how to do it appropriately in R (today)
Iterating across data frame columns (today)
Iterating using map and walk for iteration, instead of a for loop (next lesson)

Purposes
Creating or saving a new object

Performing an action with a return output
Ex. creating new variables/datasets, fitting models, etc.
We’ll need to consider storage (memory allocation).
Next class, we’ll use map() for this…

Side effects

Performing an action without a R return output
Ex: saving data using write_csv() or saving a plot with png()

We don’t need to worry about storage in R.
We could use walk() for this…

title: Loops and Iteration
text:
for Loops
In R, for loops have the following general structure:

Codefor (i in some_vector) {
    # Code to do stuff based on i
}


some_vector can be any vector, including:

An indexing integer vector: 1:3 [Most common!]
A character vector: c("group1", "group2", "group3")

A vector of any other class


Codegroups <- c("group1", "group2", "group3") # a vector to iterate over

for (i in 1:3) { # i: index
    print(groups[i])
}

    print(g)
}

[1] "group2"

Indexing
To iterate over an indexing vector, it is useful to know about the following two functions:


seq_along(v): generates an integer sequence from 1 to the length of the vector v supplied

seq_len(n): generates an integer sequence from 1 to n



Codefor (i in seq_along(groups)) {
    print(groups[i])
}

[1] "group1"
[1] "group2"
[1] "group3"

    print(groups[i])
}

[1] "group1"
[1] "group2"
[1] "group3"


A nice feature of seq_along() is that it generates an empty iteration vector if the vector you’re iterating over itself has length 0.

seq_along(no_groups)

integer(0)

Store Output
Indexing is particularly important when we want to create/save new objects as we need to store output created during a for loop.






When using a for loop to create/save output, we should create storage containers ahead of time with the vector() function. This allocates memory for the output and is a more efficient use of memory.

✏️ Fit Stratified Models
On the diamonds dataset, fit stratified models of price vs. carat, model separately estimated for each value of cut, and store the fitted models in a list storage container.

Code# for loop
data(diamonds)

# Fit models of price vs. carat separately for each value of cut
unique_cuts <- diamonds |> pull(cut) |> levels()
lin_mod_results <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(unique_cuts))

for (i in seq_along(unique_cuts)) {
    this_cut <- unique_cuts[i]
    diamonds_sub <- diamonds |>
        filter(cut==this_cut)
    # The double square brackets [[i]] accesses the ith element of a list
    lin_mod_results[[i]] <- lm(price ~ carat, data = diamonds_sub)
}

title: Loops and Iteration
text:
Case Study
One of my most common use cases for writing functions and iteration/looping is to perform some exploration or modeling repeatedly for several different “settings”.
For example, our broad goal might be to fit a linear regression model to our data. However, there are often multiple choices that we have to make in practice:

Keep missing values or fill them in (imputation)?
Fit the model only on a certain group of cases?
Filter out outliers in one or more variables?
Transform certain variables? (e.g., log transformation)

We can map any number of these choices to arguments in a custom model-fitting function:


impute: TRUE or FALSE

filter_to: This could be a string description like “All cases”, “Group 1”, or “Groups 1 and 2”


Codefit_model <- function(data, impute, filter_to) {
    if (impute) {
        data <- some_imputation_function(data)
    }

    if (filter_to=="Group 1") {
        data <- data |>
            filter(group == 1)
    } else if (filter_to == "Groups 1 and 2") {
        data <- data |>
            filter(group %in% c(1,2))
    }

    lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data)
}


The tidyr package has a useful function called crossing() that is useful for generating argument combinations.
For each argument, we specify all possible values for that argument. crossing() generates all combinations:

Codedf_arg_combos <- crossing(
    impute = c(TRUE, FALSE),
    filter_to = c("All cases", "Group 1", "Groups 1 and 2")

Iteration with purrr

purrr is a tidyverse package that provides several useful functions for iteration.
Open up the purrr cheatsheet.
The main advantages of purrr include:

Improved readability of R code

Iteration with map

In purrr, we can use the family of map() functions to iteratively apply a function to each element of a list or vector and save its output.

Reminder: Data frames/tibbles are named lists so the elements are the “columns” so map() can iterate over columns of a dataset.

Let’s look at the purrr cheatsheet to look at graphical representations of how these functions work.


map() returns a list

map_chr() returns a character vector

map_lgl() returns a logical vector

map_int() returns an integer vector

map_dbl() returns a numeric vector

map_vec() returns a vector of a different (non-atomic) type (like dates)

Replicate str()

Let’s return to our original task to replicate str().
To get the class() of each data frame column, map_chr() is sensible because classes are strings:

Iteration with map2 or pmap

If you need to iterate over the rows of a data frame, we’ll need other versions of map().
purrr also offers map2() and the pmap() family of functions that take multiple inputs and loops over them simultaneously.
Let’s look at the purrr cheatsheet to look at graphical representations of how these functions work.
Let’s look at this code to randomly simulate data from Normal distributions.

Codeargs <- tibble(
  n = c(100, 100, 100, 100), # this is n
  mean = c(0, 1, 2, 3),            # this is mean
  sd = c(4, 3, 2, 1)            # this is sd
)

sim_data <- args |>
  mutate(rand_data = pmap(args, rnorm))

sim_data |> head() |> print()

title: NYT and Census APIs
text:
APIs
An API stands for Application Programming Interface, and this term describes a general class of tools that allows computer software, rather than humans, to interact with an organization’s data.


Application refers to software.

Interface can be thought of as a contract of service between two applications. This contract defines how the two communicate with each other using requests and responses.

Every API has documentation for how software developers should structure requests for data / information and in what format to expect responses.

title: NYT and Census APIs
text:
Web APIs
Web APIs, or Web Application Programming Interfaces, which focus on transmitting requests and responses for raw data through a web browser.

Our browsers communicate with web servers using a technology called HTTP or Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
Programming languages such as R can also use HTTP to communicate with web servers.

URL
Every document on the Web has a unique address. This address is known as Uniform Resource Locator (URL).
Every URL has the same general structure. Let’s look at this example:
https://api.census.gov/data/2019/acs/acs1?get=NAME,B02015_009E,B02015_009M&for=state:*


https://api.census.gov: This is the base URL.


http://: The scheme, which tells your browser or program how to communicate with the web server. This will typically be either http: or https:.

api.census.gov: The hostname or host address, which is a name that identifies the web server that will process the request.



data/2019/acs/acs1: The file path, which tells the web server how to get to the desired resource.

?get=NAME,B02015_009E,B02015_009M&for=state:*: The query string or query parameters, which provide the parameters for the function you would like to call.

This is a string of key-value pairs separated by &. That is, the general structure of this part is key1=value1&key2=value2.





key
value



get
NAME,B02015_009E,B02015_009M


for
state:*


Examples
A large variety of web APIs provide data. Almost all reasonably large commercial websites offer Web APIs. Todd Motto has compiled an expansive list of Public Web APIs on GitHub. Browse this list to see what data sources are available.

title: NYT and Census APIs
text:
Wrapper Packages
In R, it is easiest to access Web APIs through a wrapper package, an R package written specifically for a particular Web API.

The R development community has already contributed wrapper packages for most large Web APIs.
To find a wrapper package, search the web for “R package” and the name of the website. For example:

Searching for “R Reddit package” returns RedditExtractor

Searching for “R Weather.com package” returns weatherData




rOpenSci also has a good collection of wrapper packages.

In our work with maps, we’ve used the tidycensus package to obtain census data to display on maps. tidycensus is a wrapper package that makes it easy to obtain desired census information:

Codetidycensus::get_acs(
    year = 2020,
    state = "MN",
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c("B01003_001", "B19013_001"),
    output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE
)


What is going on behind the scenes with get_acs()? Let’s look at how to access Web API’s directly with URL’s.

title: NYT and Census APIs
text:
Access Web APIs Directly
Get a Census API Key
Many APIs require users to obtain a key to use their services.

This lets organizations keep track of what data is being used.
It also rate limits their API and ensures programs don’t make too many requests per day/minute/hour. Be aware that most APIs do have rate limits — especially for their free tiers.

The U.S. Census Data API required (free) key registration when passing the Query Limits. To obtain a key, navigate to https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html and enter your information as follows:

Organization: Macalester College
Email: Your Mac email address

You will get the message:

Your request for a new API key has been successfully submitted. Please check your email. In a few minutes you should receive a message with instructions on how to activate your new key.

Check your email. Copy and paste your key into a new text file:

File > New File > Text File (towards the bottom of the menu)
Save as census_api_key.txt in the same folder as this .qmd. 📌 Don’t commit this file to GitHub. Make Git ignores it via GitHub Desktop (Right click the file –> select Ignore file (add to .gitignore).

Read in the key with the following code:

Codecensus_api_key <- readLines("census_api_key.txt")

# if you will be below the query limit, you can pass an empty key as follows
census_api_key <- ""


Navigate API Documentation
Navigate to the Census API user guide and click on the “Example API Queries” tab. Let’s look at the Population Estimates Example and the American Community Survey (ACS) Example. These examples walk us through the steps to incrementally build up a URL to obtain desired data. This URL is known as a web API request.
https://api.census.gov/data/2019/acs/acs1?get=NAME,B02015_009E,B02015_009M&for=state:*
For this request,

we can adjust the path to change desired dataset (acs1) and year
we can adjust the query string to get different variables (get) and for different states (for)

?get=NAME,B02015_009E,B02015_009M&for=state:*
Typically, each of these URL components will be specified in the API documentation. Sometimes, the scheme, hostname, and path (https://api.census.gov/data/2019/acs/acs1) will be referred to as the endpoint for the API call.
Build a URL with httr2

We will use the httr2 package to build up a full URL from its parts because of URLs need to be percent encoded.


request() creates an API request object using the base URL


req_url_path_append() builds up the URL by adding path components separated by /


req_url_query() adds the ? separating the endpoint from the query and sets the key-value pairs in the query

The .multi argument controls how multiple values for a given key are combined.
The I() function around "state:*" inhibits parsing of special characters like : and *. (It’s known as the “as-is” function.)
The backticks around for are needed because for is a reserved word in R (for for-loops). You’ll need backticks whenever the key name has special characters (like spaces, dashes).
We can see from here that providing an API key is achieved with key=YOUR_API_KEY.




Codereq <- request("https://api.census.gov") |>
    req_url_path_append("data") |>
    req_url_path_append("2019") |>
    req_url_path_append("acs") |>
    req_url_path_append("acs1") |>
    req_url_query(
        get = c("NAME", "B02015_009E", "B02015_009M"), 
        `for` = I("state:*"), 
        key = census_api_key, 
        .multi = "comma"
    )


Why would we ever use these steps instead of just using the full URL as a string?

To generalize this code with functions!
To handle special characters

e.g., query parameters might have spaces, which need to be represented in a particular way in a URL (URLs can’t contain spaces)


Send a Request with httr2

Once we’ve fully constructed our request, we can use req_perform() to send out the API request and get a response.

Coderesp <- req_perform(req)


Parse a Response with httr2

We see from Content-Type that the format of the response is something called JSON. We can navigate to the request URL to see the structure of this output.

We can use resp_body_json() in httr2 to parse the JSON into a nicer R format.

This function uses fromJSON() behind the scenes.
Without simplifyVector = TRUE, the JSON is read in as a list.




Coderesp_json_df <- resp |> resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)

# Data Cleaning
resp_json_df <- janitor::row_to_names(resp_json_df, 1) |> # Move 1st row to Names
  as.data.frame() |> # Convert Matrix to Data Frame
  mutate(across(starts_with('B'), as.numeric)) # Convert all variables that start with B to numeric

title: NYT and Census APIs
text:
New York Times API
This example will build on the New York Times Web API, which provides access to news articles, movie reviews, book reviews, and many other data.
We will specifically focus on the Article Search API, which finds information about news articles that contain a particular word or phrase.
Get an Authentication Key
To get started with the NY Times API, you must register and get an authentication key. Signup only takes a few seconds, and it lets the New York Times make sure nobody abuses their API for commercial purposes. It also rate limits their API and ensures programs don’t make too many requests per day. For the NY Times API, this limit is 1000 calls per day.
Once you have signed up, verified your email, log back in to https://developer.nytimes.com. Under your email address, click on Apps and Create a new App (call it First API) and enable Article Search API, then press Save. This creates an authentication key, which is a 32 digit string with numbers and the letters a-e.
As with your census API key, save this key in a .txt file, and read it in and store this in a variable called times_key. 📌 Again, don’t commit this file to GitHub. Make Git ignores it via GitHub Desktop (Right click the file –> select Ignore file (add to .gitignore).

Codetimes_key <- read_lines("nyt_api_key.txt")


Build a URL
Open this URL in your browser (you should replace MY_KEY with the API key you were given).
https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json?q=gamergate&api-key=1GGtS3Z19aPC6z6BwuglQ404urUOFOFIZPcXteMltvp9imcO
The text you see in the browser is the response data (in JSON format).
This URL has the same structure that we discussed above for the census API:


https:// — The scheme, which tells your browser or program how to communicate with the web server. This will typically be either http: or https:.

api.nytimes.com — The hostname, which is a name that identifies the web server that will process the request.

/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json — The path, which tells the web server what function you would like to call (a function for searching articles).

?q=gamergate&api-key=MY_KEY — The query parameters, which provide the parameters for the function you would like to call. The key value pairs are the following:



key
value



q
gamergate


api-key
MY_KEY



The scheme, hostname, and path (https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json) together form the endpoint for the API call.
We can use the httr2 package to build up a full URL from its parts:

Codereq <- request("https://api.nytimes.com") |>
    req_url_path_append("svc") |>
    req_url_path_append("search") |>
    req_url_path_append("v2") |>
    req_url_path_append("articlesearch.json") |>
    req_url_query(q = "gamergate", `api-key` = times_key)


We can write a function to generate the URL for a user-specified query.

Codecreate_nyt_url <- function(query, key) {
    request("https://api.nytimes.com") |>
        req_url_path_append("svc") |>
        req_url_path_append("search") |>
        req_url_path_append("v2") |>
        req_url_path_append("articlesearch.json") |>
        req_url_query(q = query, `api-key` = key)
}


Let’s use this function to find articles related to:


Ferris Bueller's Day Off (note the spaces and the apostrophe)

Penn & Teller (note the spaces and the punctuation mark &)


Codereq_fb <- create_nyt_url(query = "Ferris Bueller's Day Off", key = times_key)
req_pt <- create_nyt_url(query = "Penn & Teller", key = times_key)


We can use req_perform() to send out the request and resp_body_json() to parse the resulting JSON.

Coderesp_pt <- req_pt |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json(simplifyVector = TRUE)


Explore Complex Lists
resp_pt is a list. A list is a useful structure for storing elements of different types. Data frames are special cases of lists where each list element has the same length (but where the list elements have different classes).
Lists are a very flexible data structure but can be very confusing because list elements can be lists themselves!
We can explore the structure of a list in two ways:

Entering View(list_object) in the Console. The triangle buttons on the left allow you to toggle dropdowns to explore list elements.
Using the str() (structure) function.

Using base R subsetting, we can access elements of a list in three ways:

By position with double square brackets [[:


Code# This gets the first element of the list
resp_pt[[1]]



By name with double square brackets [[: (note that list elements are not always named, so this won’t always be possible)


Code# Accessing by name directly
resp_pt[["status"]]

# Accessing via a variable
which_element <- "status"
resp_pt[[which_element]]



By name with a dollar sign $: (Helpful tip: For this mode of access, RStudio allows tab completion to fill in the full name)


Coderesp_pt$status


We can retrieve these nested attributes by sequentially accessing the object keys from the outside in. For example, the meta element would be accessed as follows:

Coderesp_pt$response$meta

title: Am I Actually Getting Better at the Waffle?
text:
One of my best friends lives in Dubai, and since most video-calling over apps is banned, I Google Meet her once a month. Google Meet can lead to some interesting screen-sharing opportunities; we added the New York Times games suite into our calls every month, and we added a game called Waffle to our rotation shortly after (see example of a Waffle Deluxe board below).



The goal of the game is to find all eight words in as few letter swaps as possible (must be fewer than 26 swaps), as fast as possible. Every call (we called about once a month) we would play three rounds of this game (except for December 2025, we only played 2 rounds), and record how long it took us to play the game. I originally just used Google Sheets to give me an overall average time with and without outliers, but I have other questions: how has our average changed over time? Have we actually gotten better? Are we worse at the first round than the third round? Let’s answer these questions!

View Set-up and Data#Install and Load packages
#install.packages("googlesheets4")
#install.packages("kableExtra") 
library(googlesheets4)
library(tidyverse)
library(rstatix)
library(plotly)
library(kableExtra)
library(knitr)

# Authorize with the Sheets scope
#gs4_auth(scopes = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.readonly")

#Read in the data
waffle = read_sheet("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1d5EpYRwLbhHzg88ndTDWJOECDkzzC_KcmPcgN9tvkNY/edit?gid=0#gid=0")
waffle$date = as.Date(waffle$date)
waffle$round = as.factor(waffle$round)



View Summary Table Code#Average time by date 
summary = waffle %>%
  group_by(date)%>%
  summarize(average_time = mean(time, na.rm=TRUE), 
            sd_time = sd(time, na.rm = TRUE))

#Excluding extreme points
outlier = identify_outliers(waffle, time)
waffle_new = waffle %>%
  filter(!(date == outlier$date & time == outlier$time))

#Re-calculate average time by date 
summary_new = waffle_new %>%
  group_by(date)%>%
  summarize(average_time = mean(time, na.rm=TRUE), 
            sd_time = sd(time, na.rm = TRUE))

#Disaggregated with outliers 
average_old = mean(waffle$time, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_old = sd(waffle$time, na.rm = TRUE)

#Disaggregated without outliers 
average_new = mean(waffle_new$time, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_new = sd(waffle_new$time, na.rm = TRUE)

#Aggregate at the round level 
rounds = waffle%>%
  group_by(round)%>%
  summarize(mean_time = mean(time, na.rm=TRUE), 
            sd_time = sd(time, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
  rename(`Round` = round)

#Aggregate at the round level without the outlier
rounds_new = waffle_new%>%
  group_by(round)%>%
  summarize(mean_time = mean(time, na.rm=TRUE), 
            sd_time = sd(time, na.rm=TRUE))%>%
      rename(`Round` = round)

#Create a summary Table by date
table_date = full_join(
  summary %>%
    rename(`Average Time (With Outliers)` = average_time,
      `Variability in Time (With Outliers)` = sd_time, 
      `Date` = date),
  summary_new %>%
    rename(`Average Time (Without Outliers)` = average_time,
      `Variability in Time (Without Outliers)` = sd_time, 
      `Date` = date),
  by = "Date")

table_date %>%
  kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c(
      "Date",

    ),

From our descriptive statistics, we see that the average time it takes to solve a Deluxe waffle falls, and we are more consistently doing doing better (our variability falls as well). Additionally, once we exclude outliers, our third round is better than our second round, which is better than our first - we are about 50 seconds faster at solving a waffle the third time around than the first. Let’s look at some graphs. The first set of graphs is with outliers, and the second is without.
Graphing with Outliers
These graphs tell me that I have gotten so so much better at this game. I reduce my average time by 50%, and I get more consistent.

View Graphing Codeggplot(summary, aes(x = date, y = average_time)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")+
  labs(x = "Date Game Played", y = "Average Time (minutes)", title = "Average Time Taken to Solve a Waffle", subtitle = "The average time to solve a deluxe waffle falls by over 50%, from about 12 minutes \nin January 2026 to under 6 minutes in September 2026.", caption = "Date Created: September 24, 2026 | Author: Tanisha Dodla")






View Graphing Codeggplot(summary, aes(x = date, y = sd_time)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+

Graphing without Outliers
When we remove an outlier time of 19 minutes spent in January 2026 (using the IQR method, but with a tolerance of 3 instead of 1.5), we get very different results. These next three graphs show a more stable trend: we don’t seem to be doing any better, but we also don’t seem to be doing any worse. If anything, we seem to be more consistently doing just medium.

View Graphing Codeggplot(summary_new, aes(x = date, y = average_time)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")+
  labs(x = "Date Game Played", y = "Average Time (minutes)", title = "Average Time Taken to Solve a Waffle Without Extreme Outliers", subtitle = "The average time stays roughly the same, from about 5 minutes \nin January 2026 to just under 5 minutes in September 2026.", caption = "Date Created: September 24, 2026 | Author: Tanisha Dodla")






View Graphing Codeggplot(summary_new, aes(x = date, y = sd_time)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")+
  labs(x = "Date Game Played", y = "Standard Deviation of Time (minutes)", title = "Variability in Time Taken to Solve a Waffle without Extreme Outliers", subtitle = "The standard deviation between solve times for the deluxe waffle falls, from about 3 minutes \nin February 2026 to under 1 minute in September 2026.", caption = "Date Created: September 24, 2026 | Author: Tanisha Dodla")






View Graphing Codeggplot(waffle_new, aes(
  x = date,
  y = time,
  color = round,
  group = round)) +
  geom_line()+
  theme_classic()+
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")+
  labs(x = "Date Game Played", y = "Time (minutes)", title = "Time Taken to Solve a Waffle, Colored by Round, Without Extreme Outliers", subtitle = "The first round is the most variable.", caption = "Date Created: September 24, 2026 | Author: Tanisha Dodla", color = "Round Played")







This exercise has shown me that not including outliers may completely change the trend that I see. It has also shown me that I haven’t really gotten better or worse - just more consistent. I guess that means that I should play more (I’m certainly not getting any worse)!

title: My Listening History: Spotify Data
text:
Set-up Code#Load Packages 
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(lubridate)
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)

music_0 = fromJSON("../extra/Spotify Account Data/StreamingHistory_music_0.json")
music_1 = fromJSON("../extra/Spotify Account Data/StreamingHistory_music_1.json")

music = bind_rows(music_0, music_1)


Artists over Time
I wanted to first look at my most listened to artists over time. There are two ways to look at this, given the data I have. I could track listening time by minutes listened, or I could track listening time by number of plays. I do both, because some tracks are longer (have longer listening times but fewer plays) and some tracks are shorter (have shorter listening times but more plays) and compare the results.
Listening Time

Data Wrangling Codemusic = music %>%
  mutate(endTime = ymd_hm(endTime),
    month = as.Date(floor_date(endTime, "month")),
    minutesPlayed = msPlayed / 60000)

top_artists= music %>%
  group_by(artistName) %>%
  summarise(total_minutes = sum(minutesPlayed, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  slice_max(total_minutes, n = 10)

music_top = music %>%
  filter(artistName %in% top_artists$artistName) %>%
  mutate(month = as.Date(floor_date(endTime, "month")))

monthly_artist = music_top %>%
  group_by(month, artistName) %>%
  summarise(minutesPlayed = sum(minutesPlayed, na.rm = TRUE), plays = n(), .groups = "drop")



Graphing Codeggplot(
  monthly_artist,
  aes(x = month, y = minutesPlayed, color = artistName)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha=0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 month",
    date_labels = "%b\n%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "My Listening Habits in the Last Year",
    subtitle = "Top 10 artists by total listening time",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Minutes Played",
    color = "Artist"
  ) +
  theme_classic()







From looking at my 10 most listened to artists in the last year, there is a very clear pattern of me suddenly becoming obsessed with an artist, and then gradually stop listening to them. This phenomenon seems to be most pronounced with Saint Levant, but can also be seen with Rosalía and Sasha Alex Sloan. However, if I were to have access to all of my Spotify data, this sudden spike in listening would not be super obvious (I listened to these artists, but it was more than a year ago, so this data does not reflect that). On the other hand,I listen to Pritam, Sabrina Carpenter, and Charli xcx fairly consistently, with peaks when they release new albums or singles.
Number of Plays

Data Wrangling Codetop_artists1 = music %>%
  group_by(artistName) %>%
  summarise(total_plays = n()) %>%
  slice_max(total_plays, n = 10)

music_top1 = music %>%
  filter(artistName %in% top_artists1$artistName) %>%
  mutate(month = as.Date(floor_date(endTime, "month")))

monthly_artist1 = music_top1 %>%
  group_by(month, artistName) %>%
  summarise(minutesPlayed = sum(minutesPlayed, na.rm = TRUE), plays = n(), .groups = "drop")



Graphing Codeggplot(
  monthly_artist1,
  aes(x = month, y = plays, color = artistName)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha=0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 month",
    date_labels = "%b\n%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "My Listening Habits in the Last Year",
    subtitle = "Top 10 artists by number of plays",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of Plays",
    color = "Artist"
  ) +
  theme_classic()







The same sudden listening followed by a gradual drop-off phenomenon is seen here too, but with slightly different artists: Saint Levant stays, but we see it this time with Rosalía and t.A.T.u. We also see some new artists here: Zara Larsson and Tate McRae make an appearrance, and Charli xcx and Brahms are no longer on the list. Rosalía being consistent in the minutes listened graph but sudden in the number of plays chart indicates to me that her songs are shorter than other songs produced by these artists (this is somewhat true, but especially true of the songs of hers that I listen to on repeat).
Songs over Time
I do the same analysis (by listening time and number of plats), but I now do this by top 10 songs.
Listening Time

Data Wrangling Codetop_songs = music %>%
  group_by(trackName, artistName) %>%
  summarise(
    total_minutes = sum(minutesPlayed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  slice_max(total_minutes, n = 10)

music_top_songs = music %>%
